summary: Find a target in a sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot, in O(log n).
mainInsight: At every step at least one half of [lo, hi] is sorted. Identify the sorted half by comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid], check whether the target lies in that half, and discard the other half.

approaches.name: Single modified binary search
approaches.summary: Decide which half is sorted and whether the target falls in it.

personalSolution.approach: Single modified binary search (>= for the sorted-left test, elif for the sorted-right test)
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. The `elif` for the right half is only reached when the left half is unsorted; a plain `else` expresses that more safely.

commonMistakes: Using < instead of <= when comparing lo and mid
Wrong boundary for the target range test
Assuming the array has no rotation

promptVariants: How does binary search work on a rotated sorted array?
What do you decide at each step?
options: Find the sorted half, test the target against it, then discard
Sort the array first and then run a normal binary search
Always search the left half only, because it is the larger one
Compare the target with the first element, then scan linearly
cards.answer: Find the sorted half, test the target against it, then discard
cards.explanation: One of the two halves is always sorted, which gives a reliable range test.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Always search the left half only, becaus: Either half may hold the target.

promptVariants: How do you know which half is sorted and when to go into it?
Why is the comparison `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` used?
cards.answer: If nums[lo] <= nums[mid] the left half [lo, mid] is sorted (the <= handles lo == mid). Then go left if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], otherwise right. Symmetrically, when the right half is sorted go right if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], else left.
keyPoints: Range test on the sorted half
Else go to the other half
cards.explanation: Duplicates break this (Search in Rotated Sorted Array II).

promptVariants: Your left-half test is `nums[mid] >= nums[lo]` and the right-half branch is an `elif`. What happens for nums = [3, 1], target = 1 if the test is changed to `>`?
Why must the sorted-left test include equality?
cards.answer: With nums = [3, 1], lo = 0 and mid = 0, so nums[mid] == nums[lo]. With `>` the left branch is skipped, and the elif `nums[mid] <= nums[hi]` is 3 <= 1, which is false, so neither branch runs, lo and hi never change, and the loop never ends. With `>=` the one-element left half [3] is treated as sorted and the search moves right to index 1.
keyPoints: Wrong test leaves both branches untaken (infinite loop)
cards.explanation: Equality in the sorted-half test is what handles the smallest ranges.
Half of the range is discarded each step.

promptVariants: What is the two-pass alternative to the single modified binary search?
How would you solve it by finding the pivot first?
cards.answer: Binary search for the pivot (the index of the minimum, where nums[mid] > nums[hi] sends you right), then run an ordinary binary search on whichever sorted part can contain the target (or on the whole array with indices shifted by the pivot). Still O(log n) time and O(1) space, but two loops with their own boundary conditions.
keyPoints: Normal binary search on the right part
cards.explanation: The single-pass version is shorter once the sorted-half idea is clear.
